html:
1What You Will Learn

Note

Acronyms in this note. SDK: software development kit

  • Prompt chaining (fixed sequential steps) versus dynamic, adaptive decomposition
  • Splitting a large review into per-file passes plus a cross-file integration pass
  • Decomposing an open-ended task by mapping first, then planning
  • Named session resumption, fork_session, and when to start fresh with a summary instead of resuming

2Choosing a Decomposition Strategy

Running case

Birchwood Supply Reviews a Big Change

  • A pull request changes 12 files of the checkout module
  • A separate request asks the agent to "add tests to the legacy order system", a codebase nobody fully understands
  • The two jobs need different ways of breaking work down
Prompt chaining (fixed pipeline) Dynamic adaptive decomposition
Idea Break the job into known sequential steps; each step's output feeds the next Let what you discover decide the next subtasks
Use when The aspects are predictable: multi-aspect reviews, standard report building The task is open-ended: unfamiliar code, investigations
Example Analyze each file, then run a cross-file integration pass Map the structure, find high-impact areas, write a prioritized plan, adapt as dependencies appear

Exam tip

"Predictable aspects" → prompt chaining. "Unfamiliar, open-ended" → dynamic decomposition.

Reviewing many files: local passes plus an integration pass

  • One pass over 12 files gives uneven depth (thorough for some files, shallow for others), missed bugs and contradictory feedback (a pattern flagged in one file and approved in another). The cause is attention dilution.
  • Fix: one focused pass per file for local issues, then a separate integration pass for cross-file data flow and interfaces.
  • A bigger context window, or asking developers to shrink the pull request, does not fix the quality of attention; and requiring 2 of 3 runs to agree would hide real bugs found only once.

Open-ended tasks ("add tests to the legacy system")

  1. Map the structure (modules, entry points).
  2. Identify high-impact areas (critical or untested code).
  3. Create a prioritized plan.
  4. Work through it and adapt as new dependencies are discovered.
Exam tip

A big pull request reviewed unevenly means attention dilution: per-file passes plus an integration pass, not a bigger context window.

3Session State, Resumption and Forking (Task 1.7)

A session is the stored conversation (prompts, tool calls, results). You can come back to it later.

Need Use Command or option
Continue a specific named investigation across work sessions Named session resumption claude --resume <session-name> (give names with claude -n "name" or /rename)
Try two approaches from the same analyzed baseline fork_session claude --resume <id> --fork-session (SDK: resume + forkSession)
Prior context is mostly still valid Resume Add a note about what changed
Prior tool results are stale (files changed) Start a new session with an injected structured summary Summary of findings, not raw old output

  • Fork creates independent branches from a shared baseline, for example comparing two testing strategies or two refactorings. Each branch keeps its own history; the original is unchanged.
  • When you resume after code changes, tell the agent which files changed so it re-analyzes just those, rather than trusting stale reads or re-exploring everything.
  • Why a fresh session with a summary can beat a resume: old tool results may no longer match the files, and the model may keep acting on them.
claude -n "checkout-review"                      # name the session when you start it
claude --resume "checkout-review"                # continue it later
claude --resume "checkout-review" --fork-session # branch it to try another approach

[Verify live] In current Claude Code, --resume accepts a session ID or name, --fork-session creates a new session ID when resuming, and the Agent SDK offers resume and fork_session / forkSession options. A fork branches the conversation, not the files: edits made in a fork are real. As of 8 November 2026.

Exam tip

Stale results after code changes: tell the resumed session which files changed, or start fresh with a summary. Never trust old tool output.

4Exam Q&A

S1A pull request changes 12 files, and a single-pass review gives deep feedback on some files, shallow comments on others, and contradicts itself across files. How should the review be restructured?

  • ARun the same full pass three times and keep only the issues that were found at least twice
  • BRun focused per-file passes for local issues, then one integration pass across files
  • CRequire authors to split every pull request into 3 to 4 files
  • DSwitch to a model with a larger context window
Show the answer

Answer: B. The problem is attention dilution. Per-file passes plus an integration pass give consistent depth and still catch cross-file issues.

S2For which task is dynamic adaptive decomposition the best fit?

  • AConverting 500 files with an identical mechanical edit
  • BGenerating the same standard report from a fixed template every night for the finance team
  • CAdding tests to an unfamiliar legacy codebase where dependencies emerge along the way
  • DRunning a fixed three-step review on each pull request
Show the answer

Answer: C. Open-ended work needs a plan that adapts to what is discovered. The others are predictable.

S3A team wants a repeatable analysis for every pull request: security, style, tests, then a summary. The aspects never change. Which strategy fits?

  • AUse a different, random order of steps for each pull request
  • BA single huge prompt with no steps
  • CFully dynamic decomposition
  • DPrompt chaining with a fixed sequence of steps
Show the answer

Answer: D. Predictable multi-aspect work, with aspects that never change, suits a fixed chain of steps.

S4An engineer analyzed a payment module yesterday in a named session. Overnight, two files changed. What is the best way to continue?

  • AResume the named session and tell the agent which two files changed
  • BStart a brand-new session and re-read all 300 files in the repository from scratch
  • CDelete the session and rely on memory
  • DResume and say nothing; the agent will notice
Show the answer

Answer: A. The prior context is mostly valid; informing the agent of the changed files gives targeted re-analysis.

S5After a week, a session's saved tool results come from a repository that has been heavily refactored. What is the most reliable approach?

  • AOnly ask short questions
  • BStart a new session and inject a structured summary of the earlier findings, then verify against the current code
  • CFork the session and keep the stale results
  • DResume the session and trust the old tool results, because they were correct when they were read
Show the answer

Answer: B. Stale tool results are risky; a fresh session seeded with a summary is more reliable than resuming.

S6An engineer wants to compare a refactor to repository classes with a refactor to service classes, both starting from the same codebase analysis. Which mechanism fits?

  • Afork_session to branch independently from the shared baseline
  • BTwo unrelated new sessions that each repeat the whole codebase analysis
  • C--continue twice
  • DOne session where both approaches are mixed together in a single conversation
Show the answer

Answer: A. Forking branches from a shared analysis so each approach develops separately.

S7What does a fork of a session branch?

  • AThe model weights, so each branch trains on its own edits
  • BThe conversation history; edited files remain shared
  • CThe files on disk
  • DThe user's permissions only
Show the answer

Answer: B. Forking copies the conversation, not the file system; file edits in a fork are real.

S8Which TWO tasks are best served by dynamic adaptive decomposition? Select TWO.

  • ARunning the same linter on every file
  • BInvestigating an unexplained slowdown across several services
  • CApplying an identical mechanical edit to 500 files
  • DAdding tests to an unfamiliar legacy codebase
  • EA nightly report from a fixed template
Show the answer

Answer: B, D. Open-ended work where each finding changes the next step needs an adaptive plan. Templates, linting and mechanical edits follow predictable steps.

5Quick Reference Card

Topic Key fact
Prompt chaining Fixed sequential steps for predictable multi-aspect work
Dynamic decomposition Plan adapts to discoveries; for open-ended tasks (map → prioritize → adapt)
Large review Per-file local passes + integration pass (cures attention dilution)
Resume --resume <name>; tell the agent which files changed
Fork fork_session / --fork-session: independent branches from one baseline (conversation only)
Fresh start When tool results are stale: new session + structured summary
